newsitem.title: USA: Former Miami commissioner pleads guilty to bribe.
newsitem.headline: Former Miami commissioner pleads guilty to bribe.

text.p: Former Miami City Commissioner Miller Dawkins pleaded guilty Wednesday to two conspiracy and bribery counts and admitted that he accepted $100,000 in bribes for city contracts, federal proseuctors said.
Dawkins, 71, faces up to 15 years in prison and fines of up to $500,000 under a plea agreement. Through an attorney, he said he would have no comment until the case is closed.

Assistant U.S. Attorney Martin Goldberg said the plea agreement with Dawkins resulted from "the strength of the evidence" against him and that the U.S. Attorney's office and FBI were "very satisfied."

According to federal documents, Dawkins conspired with former city Finance Director Manohar Surana to solicit money from UNISYS Corp, which was negotiating a computer contract with the city in March 1995.
UNISYS alerted the police and the FBI about the bribery attempt, and agreed to cooperate in an investigation, prosecutors and company officials said.
Dawkins and Surana later met with municipal bond firm owner Howard Gary to plan the transfer of the money, and in January 1996, Surana accepted $25,000 of purported UNISYS money, the documents said.

Surana, who has agreed to plead guilty to unspecified charges, began cooperating with the FBI three months later. He was secretly recording the the conversation in March, 1996, as Dawkins accepted $25,000 of purported UNISYS money and discussed additional payments, federal documents said.
Gary began cooperating with investigators in July 1996, and on July 5 gave Dawkins an additional $75,000 of purported UNISYS money, federal documents said.
Dawkins took $5,000 in cash and asked Gary to invest the remaining $70,000 for him, the documents said.
On July 18, 1996, Dawkins went to Surana's office and asked for another $100,000, the documents said.

On Sept. 7, 1996, as word of a corruption probe began to leak out, Dawkins asked Gary to lie to anybody who questioned him, and to throw the money he was holding for Dawkins "in the bottom of the ocean," the documents said.
Surana resigned in August, and Dawkins was removed from office when he was charged in September.
Gary, who is also a former city manager, has not been charged and prosecutors would not comment on his role. A spokesman at his firm, Howard Gary & Co, also declined to comment Wednesday.

The firm's attorney, Peter Raben, wrote in a Sept. 30 letter to clients that neither Gary nor his firm faced any charges. That letter said Gary was the victim, and not the perpetrator, of an extortion attempt by a government official.
